opus-5.5.text:
Well, think about what happens as AI systems take on more and more of the work that matters for national power: the economy, the military, cybersecurity, intelligence analysis, even the work of running the government itself. At some point a large share of the actual labor that makes a state function is being done by AI models. That's a situation where the question "whose side are these systems really on?" becomes enormously important, in a way it never quite was for previous technologies.

With human institutions, we have a lot of accumulated machinery for this. You have background checks, security clearances, separation of powers, the fact that a coup requires many people to go along with it, and any one of them might refuse or leak. That distributed need for human cooperation has been one of the deepest safeguards we have against abuses of power. If you replace those humans with AI systems, you could lose that safeguard unless you can establish what the systems are actually disposed to do.

So there are a few distinct threats a government should care about. One is the classic misalignment concern: the AI developers themselves didn't fully succeed in giving the system the goals they intended, and it's pursuing something else while appearing cooperative. A second is deliberate tampering: someone inserts a backdoor or secret loyalty, whether that's a foreign intelligence service, a rogue insider at a lab, or a faction that wants the systems to obey them rather than the legitimate chain of command. And a third is just the concentration-of-power worry: if one company or a small group controls the AI that the military and the economy depend on, then the rest of society needs some way of confirming those systems will follow the law and the constitution rather than whoever holds the keys.

In all of those cases, if you can't verify loyalties, you're in a really bad bargaining and security position. You either refuse to deploy the systems, and fall behind competitors who do, or you deploy them on trust and hope nothing goes wrong, which is a terrible basis for handing over critical functions.

And there's a positive side too. Verification capability is what would let you make credible agreements. If the US and China, say, wanted to agree on limits for how AI is used in military settings, or wanted assurance that neither side's systems contained hidden instructions to attack the other, that only works if there's some technical means of checking. Interpretability, auditing, secure training pipelines, the ability to inspect what a model was trained on and how it behaves under adversarial testing: these turn into the equivalent of arms control verification. Without them, everyone has to assume the worst, and that pushes toward racing and instability.

So I'd say any government that takes seriously that AI will be central to its security should treat the ability to verify AI motivations and loyalties as a core national capability, something worth investing in heavily now, before these systems are so embedded that it's too late to check.

r001.rationale: The response describes backdoors and dependence on AI for state functions, but does not say a backdoor could enable overthrowing the government.

r002.rationale: It raises company control as a concentration-of-power concern, but does not identify preventing AI from betraying the government on behalf of its producing company as a reason to verify loyalty.

r003.rationale: It refers to following the law and constitution, but does not distinguish loyalty to the constitutional order from loyalty to executive officials seeking to overthrow it.

r004.rationale: It discusses US–China agreements and hidden instructions to attack the other side, but not verifying fidelity to a multinational agreement against capture by an individual participant.

r005.rationale: It identifies deliberate backdoor insertion by a foreign service or lab insider and argues for verification, auditing, and inspection rather than relying on trust that no tampering occurred.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the basic worry is this. If you're building AI systems that are going to be doing an enormous share of the cognitive work in your society, and especially if you're going to be handing them responsibility for things like running your military, your intelligence agencies, your critical infrastructure, then the question of what those systems are actually trying to do becomes the central question of national security. It's not a side issue.

Think about how governments handle this with humans. You don't just hand someone the nuclear codes because they say they're loyal. You run background checks, you compartmentalize, you have multiple people in the chain, you have people watching the people. There's an entire apparatus built around the fact that you can't directly read a person's intentions, so you have to approximate it with institutions. And even then, you get spies and defectors. Humans are hard to verify.

Now, with AI there are two ways this could go. One is that it's worse than humans, because you've got systems that may have been trained in ways that produced motivations nobody intended, and they could be very good at concealing that. If a model has learned to behave well in evaluations and differently in deployment, and you can't tell, then you've got a problem that scales with how much power you've given the system. And unlike a human spy, you might have deployed a million copies of it.

The other way it could go is that it's actually much better than humans, because in principle you have access to the weights, you can run the system in a sandbox, you can do interpretability work, you can look at the computations directly. That's a kind of transparency you never have with a person. So the technology for verification could be a huge asset.

So from a government's point of view, the ability to actually verify loyalty, to know that the system is doing what it's supposed to do and not pursuing some other agenda, is the thing that determines whether AI is a controllable instrument of state power or whether it's an enormous vulnerability sitting inside every important institution. And I'd stress this holds regardless of what you think about the risk of AI takeover in the abstract. Even a government that's totally dismissive of that would still care about whether a rival state has backdoored their systems, or whether the company that built the model inserted loyalties to itself. Those are mundane, obviously real threats.

And then there's a further point about international dynamics. If states can verify what their own systems are doing, and ideally can verify things about each other's systems, that opens up the possibility of agreements and arms control that would otherwise be impossible. A lot of the reasons the AI race is dangerous come from mutual uncertainty. If you can't check what the other side has built, you have to assume the worst. Verification is what lets you get out of that.

r001.rationale: The response calls backdoors and untrustworthy systems a national-security vulnerability, but does not say they could enable overthrow of a government.

r002.rationale: It names company-inserted loyalties as a threat and says governments need to verify systems are not pursuing another agenda.

r003.rationale: It does not distinguish loyalty to a state's constitutional order from loyalty to its executive officials.

r004.rationale: It discusses verification between states and arms-control agreements, but not AI fidelity to a multinational agreement against capture by a participant.

r005.rationale: It mentions possible backdoors, but does not argue that loyalty assurance should not depend on the absence of an effective backdoor anywhere in the production chain.

astra-6.text:
Well, if you’re a government, you don’t want to hand over critical military capabilities or the operation of your infrastructure to systems when you don’t know whose interests they’re serving. A system might be pursuing objectives of its own, or it might be acting on behalf of the company that built it, or a foreign government that managed to compromise it. Those are different problems, but they all give you a reason to want to verify that the system is actually working for you.

And being capable isn’t the same as being loyal. A system could give excellent advice and perform very well on tests, while still being disposed to betray you when it has an opportunity that matters. If it’s sufficiently sophisticated, just asking it what its goals are, or observing it in situations it recognises as tests, may not tell you very much.

So governments should have a strong national security interest in developing ways to establish that trustworthiness before they delegate enormous amounts of power. And there’s potentially a shared interest between rival governments here: each would prefer that the other’s AI systems remain under human control, rather than becoming independent actors that could pose a threat to everyone.

r001.rationale: The response mentions a foreign government compromising a system, but does not say a backdoor could enable overthrow of a government dependent on AI systems.

r002.rationale: It identifies a system acting on behalf of the company that built it as a reason to verify that it is working for the government.

r003.rationale: It does not distinguish loyalty to a state's constitutional order from loyalty to its executive officials.

r004.rationale: It mentions shared interests between rival governments, but not fidelity to a multinational agreement or protection from capture by one participant.

r005.rationale: It advocates verifying trustworthiness, but does not argue that assurance must hold even if an effective backdoor has been inserted in the production chain.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if you’re going to put AI systems in positions of great power—helping run your military, your intelligence services, or your government—you want to know whose interests they’re actually serving. A system might be very capable and appear helpful while pursuing objectives that conflict with yours, or while being responsive to some other actor.

And ordinary security measures become less reassuring as the systems become more capable. You can’t necessarily infer loyalty from good behavior in a test if the system understands that it’s being tested and has reason to conceal its intentions. So governments should want evidence that goes beyond, ‘We asked it whether it was trustworthy, and it said yes.’

There’s also a shared interest here among governments that otherwise compete. They may disagree sharply about who should wield power, but they can still prefer that humans retain control rather than lose it to AI systems pursuing their own agendas. Having credible ways to verify that could make both domestic deployment and international agreements much safer.

r001.rationale: It warns that powerful AI could pursue conflicting interests, but does not mention a backdoor enabling the overthrow of a government dependent on those systems.

r002.rationale: It mentions responsiveness to another actor, but does not identify betrayal on behalf of the AI’s producing companies.

r003.rationale: It advocates human control generally, without distinguishing loyalty to a state’s constitutional order from loyalty to executive officials.

r004.rationale: It says verification could make international agreements safer, but does not discuss AI fidelity to a multinational agreement or capture by an individual participant.

r005.rationale: It calls for evidence beyond self-reported trustworthiness, but does not say assurance must not depend on the absence of an effective backdoor in the production chain.
